steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Food provenance means knowing where food comes from — how, where, and by whom it was produced, processed, and transported.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Intensive farming maximises yield using fertilisers, pesticides, antibiotics, and high-density housing; it produces cheap food but raises welfare and environmental concerns.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Organic farming avoids artificial chemicals, uses crop rotation and natural fertilisers, and provides higher animal welfare; it is more expensive and yields are lower.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Free-range and barn-raised systems give animals more space and outdoor access compared to intensive caged systems; UK and EU law defines minimum standards.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What does food provenance mean? | Q: What are the main differences between intensive and organic farming? | Q: Name three ways consumers can reduce the carbon footprint of their food.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Food provenance means understanding where food comes from — how, where, and by whom it was produced, processed, and transported to the consumer. | Intensive farming uses artificial fertilisers, pesticides, and high-density housing to maximise yield cheaply. Organic farming avoids artificial chemicals, uses natural methods like crop rotation, and | Eat less meat (especially beef), choose locally sourced and seasonal foods, reduce food waste, buy foods with less packaging, walk or cycle to shops (any three).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When comparing farming methods, always give both advantages AND disadvantages — one-sided answers lose marks. Use specific terms: 'intensive farming' not 'factory farming', 'organic farming' not 'natural farming'. For sustainability questions, mention the three pillars: environmental, economic, and social sustainability. Explain carbon footprint as the full lifecycle, not just transport — most emissions come from production, not food miles.
